summary: Describes the Finger protocol, a simple way to ask a remote host's user information program about the people using it. A client connects and sends a short query, and the server replies with plain text about the user or the logged-in users.

plainLanguage.summary: Finger is a way to ask a remote computer about the people using it. You send one short line over TCP and the remote computer answers with readable text about the user, or about everyone who is logged in. The protocol is simple, but what it reveals can be sensitive, so the RFC spends much of its length on security.

questions: what is a ruip in finger
subtitle: A simple TCP protocol for asking a remote host about the people using it.

tldr.problem: People wanted a standard way to ask a remote computer who is logged in or to look up one user, but the original description of Finger was unclear and implementations differed.
tldr.mechanism: A client opens a TCP connection to port 79 and sends a one-line query in ASCII. The remote user information program answers with human-readable text and closes the connection.
tldr.outcome: The memo clarifies the query grammar and adds extensive security advice, because Finger discloses sensitive information about users. It obsoletes RFCs 742, 1194 and 1196.

facts.label: Data format
facts.value: ASCII, no parity, lines end in CRLF

today: RFC 1288 is a Draft Standard published in December 1991. It obsoletes RFC 742, RFC 1194 and RFC 1196, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text describes the protocol and its security risks, and says nothing about how the protocol is used today.

sections.title: Introduction and Intent
sections.content:
The memo describes the Finger user information protocol, a simple protocol that provides an interface to a remote user information program, which the document calls a RUIP. Based on RFC 742, it tries to clarify the expected communication between the two ends of a Finger connection, without invalidating the many current implementations or adding unnecessary restrictions to the original protocol definition.

The most prevalent implementations of Finger today seem to be primarily derived from the BSD UNIX work at the University of California, Berkeley, so the memo is based around the BSD version's behaviour. The BSD version provides few options to tailor the RUIP for a site's security policy, or to protect the user from dangerous data, and there are many potential security holes that implementors and administrators need to be aware of. The purpose of the protocol is to return information about a system's users, which is a sensitive issue at best, so the memo makes a number of important security comments and recommendations.

The memo also defines the words it uses for requirements. MUST, or the adjective REQUIRED, means an absolute requirement of the specification. SHOULD, or RECOMMENDED, means there may be valid reasons in particular circumstances to ignore the item, but the full implications should be understood and the case weighed first. MAY, or OPTIONAL, means the item is truly optional. An implementation is not compliant if it fails to satisfy one or more of the MUST requirements. One that satisfies all the MUST and all the SHOULD requirements is unconditionally compliant; one that satisfies all the MUST requirements but not all the SHOULD requirements is conditionally compliant.
sections.plainLanguage: Finger lets you ask a remote computer about the people using it. This memo tidies up the original description so that different implementations behave the same way, and it adds a long section on security, because the protocol hands out information about a system's users.

sections.title: History
sections.content:
The FINGER program at SAIL, written by Les Earnest, was the inspiration for the NAME program on ITS. Earl Killian at MIT and Brian Harvey at SAIL were jointly responsible for implementing the original protocol.

Ken Harrenstien is the author of RFC 742, "Name/Finger", which this memo began life as.
sections.plainLanguage: Finger grew out of the FINGER program at SAIL and the NAME program on ITS. Ken Harrenstien wrote the original specification, RFC 742, which this memo replaces.

sections.title: Flow of Events
sections.content: Finger is based on the Transmission Control Protocol, using TCP port 79 decimal (117 octal). The local host opens a TCP connection to a remote host on the Finger port. An RUIP becomes available on the remote end of the connection to process the request. The local host sends the RUIP a one line query based upon the Finger query specification and waits for the RUIP to respond. The RUIP receives and processes the query, returns an answer, then initiates the close of the connection. The local host receives the answer and the close signal, then proceeds closing its end of the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The client opens a TCP connection to port 79 on the remote host. It sends one line of text and waits. The remote program answers, closes the connection, and the client closes its side too.

sections.title: The Finger Query Specification
sections.content:
Any data transferred MUST be in ASCII format, with no parity, and with lines ending in CRLF (ASCII 13 followed by ASCII 10). This excludes other character formats such as EBCDIC, and it means that any characters between ASCII 128 and ASCII 255 should truly be international data, not 7-bit ASCII with the parity bit set.

An RUIP MUST accept the entire Finger query specification, which is defined as:

{Q1}    ::= [{W}|{W}{S}{U}]{C}
{Q2}    ::= [{W}{S}][{U}]{H}{C}
{U}     ::= username
{H}     ::= @hostname | @hostname{H}
{W}     ::= /W
{S}     ::= <SP> | <SP>{S}
{C}     ::= <CRLF>

Because {H} is recursive, there is no arbitrary limit on the number of @hostname tokens in the query. In the examples of the {Q2} request specification the number of @hostname tokens is limited to two, simply for brevity.

The query types describe the line that an RUIP actually receives, not the line a user types at an operating system prompt. If a user types "finger user@host", the RUIP on the remote host receives "user", which corresponds to {Q1}. As with anything in the IP protocol suite, the memo says to "be liberal in what you accept".
sections.plainLanguage: A query is one line of ASCII text ending in a carriage return and line feed. It can be empty, or name a user, or name a host, or both. The grammar above says exactly which forms are allowed, and a server has to accept all of them.

sections.title: Expected RUIP Response
sections.content:
For the most part, the output of an RUIP doesn't follow a strict specification, since it is designed to be read by people instead of programs. It should mainly strive to be informative.

A query of {C} is a request for a list of all online users. An RUIP MUST either answer or actively refuse. If it answers, then it MUST provide at least the user's full name. The system administrator SHOULD be allowed to include other useful information, such as terminal location, office location, office phone number, job name, and idle time, meaning the number of minutes since last typed input or since last job activity.

A query of {U}{C} is a request for in-depth status of a specified user. An answer MUST include at least the full name of the user. If the user is logged in, at least the same amount of information returned by {C} for that user MUST also be returned by {U}{C}. The system administrator SHOULD be allowed to choose to return additional useful information, such as office location, office phone number, home phone number, status of login, and user information file. A user information file is a feature wherein a user may leave a short message that will be included in the response to Finger requests, sometimes called a "plan" file.

Allowable "names" in the command line MUST include user names or login names as defined by the system. If a name is ambiguous, the system administrator SHOULD be allowed to choose whether or not all possible derivations should be returned. The token /W in the {Q1} or {Q2} query types SHOULD at best be interpreted at the last RUIP to signify a higher level of verbosity in the user information output, or at worst be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer is written for people, not for programs, so the format is loose. An empty query asks who is online; a query with a name asks about one person. The reply must at least carry the full name of each person, and the site administrator chooses how much more to add.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
Sound implementation of Finger is of the utmost importance. Implementations should be tested against various forms of attack, and an RUIP SHOULD protect itself against malformed inputs. Vendors providing Finger with the operating system or network software should subject their implementations to penetration testing. Finger is one of the avenues for direct penetration, as the Morris worm pointed out quite vividly. Like Telnet, FTP and SMTP, Finger is one of the protocols at the security perimeter of a host, so the implementation should receive just as much security scrutiny during design, implementation and testing.

The document warns that Finger discloses information about users and that such information may be considered sensitive. Security administrators should make explicit decisions about whether to run Finger and what information should be provided in responses. One existing implementation provides the time the user last logged in, the time he last read mail, whether unread mail was waiting for him, and who the most recent unread mail was from, which makes it possible to track conversations in progress and see where someone's attention was focused. Sites that are information-security conscious should not run Finger without an explicit understanding of how much information it is giving away.

The rest of the section turns into concrete recommendations. The system administrator SHOULD be given an option to turn RUIP processing of {Q2} on or off, and the default SHOULD be to refuse, because a machine that is part of a security perimeter would otherwise provide a path through it. If {Q2} processing is turned off, the RUIP MUST return a service refusal message. The same applies to {C}, with a message such as "Finger online user list denied". Implementations SHOULD let administrators tailor which atoms of information are returned, so that one administrator can return office location, office phone number, home phone number and logged in or logout time while another returns only the office location and phone number.

The document adds two warnings. Allowing an RUIP to return information out of a user-modifiable file should be seen as equivalent to allowing any information about the system to be freely distributed. Allowing an RUIP to run a user program in response to a Finger query is potentially dangerous, and the RUIP MUST NOT allow system security to be compromised by that program. A malicious user's clever or persistent use of the {U} ambiguity feature can result in a list of most of the usernames on a system, so refusal of {U} ambiguity should be considered in the same vein as refusal of {C} requests. Implementations SHOULD allow system administrators to log Finger queries.

On the client side, the client program SHOULD filter any unprintable data by default, leaving only printable 7-bit characters, ASCII 32 through ASCII 126, tabs, and CRLFs. This protects against people playing with terminal escape codes, changing other people's X window names, or committing other confusing deeds. Two separate user options SHOULD be considered to modify this behaviour, one to allow all characters less than ASCII 32 and another to allow all characters greater than ASCII 126.
sections.plainLanguage: Finger hands out information about a system's users, so it needs care on both ends. Servers should let the administrator decide what to reveal, should refuse forwarding requests by default, should not run user programs in reply to a query, and should log queries. Clients should strip out control characters before showing the answer.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content: The memo gives four worked examples. A null command line, just a carriage return and line feed, returns the list of online users with their login, full name, terminal, idle time, last login and office location. A command line naming one user, such as pirmann, returns that person's details, including office, home phone number, directory, shell, last login and any plan file. A command line naming an ambiguous user returns one block for every match. A query of type {Q2}, such as hedrick@math.rutgers.edu@pilot.njin.net, is forwarded by one host to another and the answer comes back the same way.
sections.plainLanguage: Four examples show the answers a server can return: the list of everyone online, the details of one named user, the same when the name matches several accounts, and an answer that another host fetched on request.
